t.2.72.1: Then, as Bharata, burning with grief, was preparing to set out on his journey, Śatrughna, the younger brother of Lakṣmaṇa, spoke these words to him.
t.2.72.3: That Lakṣmaṇa, who is strong and endowed with valour, why does he not set Rāma free, even if it means restraining his father?
t.2.72.2: Rāma, who in sorrow is the refuge of all beings, how much more of his own, that Rāma, rich in virtue, has been driven into exile in the forest by a woman.
t.2.72.4: But a king who has set out on the wrong path and fallen under the sway of a woman must be restrained at the very outset, once sound and unsound policy have been weighed.
t.2.72.5: While Śatrughna, the younger brother of Lakṣmaṇa, was speaking thus, the hunchbacked woman appeared at the eastern gate, adorned with every kind of ornament.
t.2.72.6: Smeared with the finest sandal paste and wearing royal garments, she, with her many-coloured girdle-strings, looked like a she-monkey tied up with ropes.
t.2.72.7: Then the doorkeeper, seeing her, the pitiless hunchbacked woman who had done great evil, seized her and reported her to Śatrughna.
t.2.72.9: And Śatrughna, deeply grieved on understanding those words, firm in his vows, spoke thus to all those who moved about the inner apartments:
t.2.72.8: She on whose account Rāma is in the forest and your father has cast off his body, here she is, wicked and cruel; deal with her as you see fit.
t.2.72.10: She by whom intense sorrow was brought upon my brothers and likewise upon my father, let this very woman reap the fruit of her cruel deed.
t.2.72.12: Then all her companions, greatly distressed and perceiving that Śatrughna was enraged, fled away in every direction.
t.2.72.11: Thus spoken of by him, the hunchbacked woman, surrounded by her companions, was swiftly and firmly seized, and she made that house resound with her cries.
t.2.72.14: Let us go for refuge to Kausalyā, who is compassionate, generous, knowing of dharma, and illustrious; may she indeed be our sure resort.
t.2.72.13: And her whole company of companions conferred together, saying, "The way this one has set about it, he will make an end of every one of us."
t.2.72.15: And Śatrughna, scorcher of foes, his eyes copper-red with rage, then dragged the hunchbacked woman, screaming, along the surface of the ground.
t.2.72.16: As Mantharā was dragged hither and thither, her many kinds of bright ornaments were scattered and broke apart upon the ground.
t.2.72.17: Strewn with those goods, the splendid royal palace then shone all the more, like the autumn sky.
t.2.72.19: Deeply distressed by those harsh and painful words, and terrified out of fear of Śatrughna, Kaikeyī came to her son for refuge.
t.2.72.18: That mighty bull among men, gripping her forcefully in his anger, rebuked Kaikeyī sharply and spoke harsh words to her.
t.2.72.20: Seeing her, Bharata said this to the enraged Śatrughna: “Women are not to be slain by any living being; let it be forgiven.”
t.2.72.21: I would kill this wicked Kaikeyī of evil conduct, if the righteous Rāma would not resent me as a matricide.
t.2.72.22: If Rāghava learns that even this hunchbacked woman has been slain, that righteous soul will surely never speak to you or to me.
t.2.72.23: Having heard the words of Bharata, Śatrughna, the younger brother of Lakṣmaṇa, then turned back from his wrath and released Mantharā.
t.2.72.24: Mantharā fell down at the feet of Kaikeyī, and, sighing and stricken with deep grief, she lamented piteously.
t.2.72.25: Seeing the hunchbacked woman, her senses stunned by Śatrughna's flinging her about, Bharata's mother gently comforted her as she looked about in distress, like a female krauñca bird caught in a snare.
